10. Under section 4(i) of the Act XL of 1958 the Senior Special Judge has the exclusive jurisdiction to take cognizance of the offence under the Prevention of Corruption Act punishable under section 5(2) of the Act II of 1947. In State represented by the Solicitor, Government of the People's Republic of Bangladesh Vs. Divisional Special Judge, Khulna Division and another 44 DLR (AD) 215 this Court re-iterated the legal provision. 

 11. After the case was transferred upon taking cognizance for an offence of criminal misconduct under section 5(i) of the Act by the Senior Special Judge under section 4(4) of the Act XL of 1958 to the Court of the Special Judge the latter has got the full panoply of powers of the trial Court like the power to frame charge or to alter or add any charge at any stage before the judgment is pronounced. The learned Counsel for the petitioner was not right in contending that the trial judge has taken cognizance of a different offence because the offence of which the Senior Special Judge had taken cognizance includes the offence for which a further charge was framed against H M Ershad. 

 19. The petitioner in Criminal Petition for Leave to Appeal No. 121 of 1992, M M Rahmatullah, was the Chairman of the RAJUK at the relevant time. His contention is that the President, as the Head of the State, in his own hand-writing passed an order for allotments of the lands in question on a petition filed by some aggrieved persons directly to him, by-passing the RAJUK and making some allegations against that authority. The petitioner as a subordinate officer was bound by the rules of business of the Government to carry out the order of the President of the country, and that his non-compliance would have amounted to insubordination. The order of allotments passed by the President was duly processed in the normal course of business in the Land and Estate Department, headed by a Member of RAJUK and after obtaining opinion from the Legal Adviser, the registration of the Lease Deed was done. The learned Judges of the High Court Division erroneously held that the petitioner illegally inserted a clause in paragraph 20 of the Lease Deed exempting the precondition of a construction before transfer, overlooking an earlier decision of the Board of Trustees dated September 2, 1986 that had waived the condition for prior construction before transfer and that decision was made long before the petitioner joined RAJUK on May 8, 1988. 

 "The scope for bribery and corruption of public servants had been enormously increased by war conditions and though the war is now over, opportunities for corrupt practices will remain for a considerable time to come. Contracts are being terminated, large amount of Government surplus stores are being disposed of; there will, for some years, be shortages of various kinds requiring the imposition of controls, and extensive schedules of postwar reconstruction, involving the disbursement of very large sums of Government money, have been and are being elaborated. All these activities offer wide scope for corrupt practices and the seriousness of the evil and the possibility of its continuance or extension in the future is such as to justify immediate and drastic action to stamp it out." (Gazette of India, 1946, Pt. V P 374) 

 The Act was intended to remain for a period of three years from its commencement under sub-section (3) of section 1 of the Act. After omission of that sub-section by section 2 of Act IX of 1950 the Prevention of Corruption Act, 1947 got a place on the Statute Book. The Criminal Law Amendment Act of 1948 (Act XIX of 1948) was passed as a complementary to that law. That Act was replaced and repealed by the Criminal Law (Amendment) Act of 1958 (Act XL of 1958) "for the more speedy trial and more effective punishment of certain offences", containing both procedural and substantive provisions. The Special Judge who administers Act II of 1947 is appointed under Act XL of 1958. Section 5 provides for the offences that are to be tried by him and a schedule of offences was appended to the Act. Item 

 This is a legislation by reference. Act II of 1947 and Act XL of 1958 are being administered together as complementary to each other for about five decades. 

 24. The decision reported in 33 DLR 379 was one under the Muslim Family Laws Ordinance, 1961 (Ordinance No. VIII of 1961) wherein no specific provision was made with regard to an offence of abetment and while summoning some of the accused for abetment, only the Ordinance was mentioned. It may be observed that abetment is an offence under the Penal Code and a person may be charged for abetting an offence made punishable by a Special Act even though abetment may not have been mentioned as an offence under the Special Act. The decision in 33 DLR 379 is to be read in that light. In the present case, abetment is specifically there in the Special Act. Though the offence of abetment was not mentioned in Act II of 1947 it was mentioned as an item in the schedule 'C' to the Criminal Law Amendment Act, 1958. Under section 5 of the Act that the Special Judge, appointed under the Act, has jurisdiction to try that offence. Besides where the prosecution case is that the offences were committed in the course of the same transaction all the accused who were alleged to have committed the offence as principals and abettors in the course of the alleged transaction can be tried under section 239 of the Code of Criminal Procedure.
